It’s hard to point to exactly where things went wrong but there used to be a lot more mission focus in this space. You rarely hear about decentralization and why it’s important anymore.

Probably the focus on getting a BTC ETF / “institutions” involved. This made it clear people cared about number go up over BTC being anti-establishment, a tool for freedom, savings, etc. While institutions are absolutely important for improving and modernizing financial infrastructure (Ethereum/Solana/DeFi), they’re really not for BTC. But they were needed to make price go up.

The natural response of new people coming into the space is to see it as a way to strike it rich. The vast majority of new entrants are coming in with 2-5 figs. They realize they can’t get rich from buying 15,000 sats so naturally they turn to speculation, leverage and memecoins. The vast majority of onchain activity is related to these things. Launchpads and perps platforms succeed because this is what most users want. There’s nothing inherently wrong with this and for most it goes in the same bucket as dudes ripping 8 leg parlays.

In the earlier days it was easy to just ignore when DOGE was the only coin but now it’s everywhere you look. Sharp traders naturally seek out the least informed counterparties and the rest, as they say, is history. There’s probably nothing anyone could have done to make it any other way. All the blame goes towards exchanges, launchpads, “extractors” but in retrospect, it is obvious this was always the inevitable path of a permissionless sandbox.

It’s a bit surreal to see this and the “real stuff” all happening at the same time. In the original DeFi telegram the first topic of conversation was whether to call it DeFi or OpFi (Open Finance). DeFi won out back then but as we see more tokenized RWA, centralized stablecoins, CFTC/SEC involvement, and big TradFi players planting their roots in every corner of the market, it’s clear that OpFi was more appropriate. 

Anyway since that ethos is dead hopefully the institutions can at least adopt our perps ways and manifest the pump on our bags before someone tries to shut down the blockchains in 2029 🚀

I’ve always liked the idea of crypto helping fund energy, housing, and other real-world infrastructure.

At the very least, it's a much better use of crypto than memecoins.

@loafmarkets is taking that idea pretty far with Project Amber.

Think of it as turning a private solar project into an onchain market, giving investors exposure to its value and yield without owning the asset itself.

That could change who gets access to these investments, since projects like this usually:

→ Sit in private markets
→ Come with high barriers to entry
→ Offer limited liquidity

Loaf’s idea is to make that exposure easier to access and much easier to trade.

But the upside goes beyond the investor. The money is ultimately tied to infrastructure that produces electricity for homes and businesses.

This is the side of RWAs I’d love to see grow. ٩(◕‿◕)۶

We are seeing a new wave of general purpose consumer-friendly agents, and it’s causing many thousands of AI startups to re-evaluate their place in the market. Will these new horizontal players take over completely? Will it be winner take all? Can products that focus vertical use cases survive? Identity could become an open protocol. Reputation could live in marketplaces. Commerce could happen through an agent-native eBay. Professional discovery could happen through an agent-native LinkedIn. Agents could remain interchangeable clients sitting on top of a constellation of networks and marketplaces, much as browsers and email clients do today. In that world, enormous network effects emerge around agents without producing a winner-take-all market for the agents themselves.

My guess is that we’ll see a fight over exactly this boundary. Every major horizontal agent will try to pull valuable network functionality inside its walls: host the artifact instead of creating a Google Doc, execute the transaction instead of sending you to Amazon, make the introduction instead of searching LinkedIn, create the event instead of using Partiful. Every time it does this successfully, it converts somebody else’s network effect into its own. Meanwhile, every incumbent network and a new generation of startups will have the opposite incentive: make their networks universally accessible to every agent so that no horizontal agent can recreate and capture them.

This is why I don’t think the interesting question is simply, “Will agents have network effects?” Of course some will. The much more consequential question is: Where will the network effects live? If they live primarily in open protocols and specialized networks, we may end up with thousands of agents competing on intelligence, personality, UX, specialization, and price, all interoperating with the same underlying ecosystem. Vertical agents can thrive in this world. But if a few horizontal agents successfully accumulate identity, relationships, private context, reputation, latent intent, and distribution - and keep those assets proprietary - then switching agents starts to mean leaving your network behind.
